title: National Income & GDP
description: Measuring an economy — output, expenditure, income approaches and what GDP misses

concepts.title: What GDP Measures
concepts.contentHtml:
Gross Domestic Product is the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a given period.

Five words do a lot of work. Market value: only things sold for money count, so unpaid housework and volunteer work don't. Final: only end products count, to avoid double-counting — a tire sold to Ford is intermediate; a tire sold at a tire shop is final. Within borders: a Toyota factory in Kentucky shows up in US GDP, not Japan's (that's GNP). In a period: GDP is a flow, not a stock — usually measured per quarter or per year.

concepts.title: Three Equivalent Approaches
concepts.contentHtml:
Every transaction has a buyer and a seller, so GDP can be measured three ways that — by accounting identity — must give the same answer.

Expenditure approach: sum of final spending. The famous identity Y = C + I + G + (X − M): consumption + investment + government + net exports. The most-quoted version.

Output (production) approach: sum of value added across all firms. Each firm's output minus the intermediate inputs it bought. Avoids double-counting automatically.

Income approach: sum of all payments to factors of production — wages, profits, interest, rents, plus indirect taxes less subsidies, plus depreciation.

The three measures rarely match exactly in practice — measurement error creates a 'statistical discrepancy' — but the equality is enforced as a long-run benchmark.

concepts.title: Nominal vs Real GDP
concepts.contentHtml:
If GDP rises 5% but prices also rose 5%, the country didn't actually produce more — it just charged more.

Nominal GDP uses current prices. Real GDP values output at the prices of a fixed base year, stripping out inflation. Real GDP is what you want when comparing across time.

The ratio between the two is the GDP deflator — a broad measure of inflation, broader than CPI because it covers everything in GDP, not just consumer goods.

Growth rates: real GDP growth captures actual changes in output. 'Growth' in macroeconomic discussion almost always means real growth.

concepts.title: GDP Per Capita & Comparisons
concepts.contentHtml:
Total GDP tells you economic size; GDP per capita tells you living standards. India's total GDP exceeds the UK's, but its per-capita GDP is roughly a fifth at PPP (closer to a twentieth at market exchange rates).

For cross-country comparisons, you also need to handle exchange rates. Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) adjusts for the fact that a dollar buys more haircuts in Manila than in Manhattan. Comparing wealth, use PPP. Comparing financial flows, use market exchange rates.

Per-capita GDP correlates strongly — though far from perfectly — with health, education, and self-reported happiness up to roughly the level of wealthy countries, after which the relationship flattens.

concepts.title: What GDP Misses
concepts.contentHtml:
GDP is the most-watched economic number, and also one of the most criticized.

Things it ignores: distribution (rising GDP can leave most people no better off), environmental damage (cutting down a forest counts as production, not loss), non-market work (childcare, eldercare, housework — overwhelmingly done by women), black/grey markets, quality changes (statisticians' hedonic adjustments only roughly capture how much better a 2025 phone is than a 2005 one), and leisure (working 80 hours instead of 40 raises GDP but not necessarily welfare).

Alternatives have been proposed — Human Development Index, Genuine Progress Indicator, Bhutan's Gross National Happiness, Stiglitz-Sen-Fitoussi recommendations — but none have replaced GDP because none combine its breadth, frequency, and comparability. Best practice: report GDP alongside other indicators, not in place of them.

title: Inflation & Unemployment
description: Price levels, the Phillips curve, NAIRU, and why both can rise together

concepts.title: Measuring Inflation
concepts.contentHtml:
Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level. Not any one price going up — that's a relative price change. Inflation is the average across the basket.

The headline measure is the Consumer Price Index (CPI): the price of a representative basket of consumer goods, tracked over time. The GDP deflator covers everything produced; core CPI strips out volatile food and energy to see the underlying trend.

None of these are perfect. CPI overstates inflation through substitution bias (when steak gets pricey, people buy chicken — but the index keeps weighting steak), quality bias (a faster computer at the same price isn't the same product), and new-goods bias (smartphones entered the basket years after they became central to spending).

concepts.title: Causes of Inflation
concepts.contentHtml:
Three classical mechanisms.

Demand-pull: aggregate demand outruns the economy's productive capacity. 'Too much money chasing too few goods.' Wartime booms, post-pandemic stimulus.

Cost-push: input costs rise — oil shocks, wage spirals, supply disruptions — and firms pass them through. The 1970s oil crises are the textbook case.

Monetary: Friedman's claim that 'inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon.' Central banks expanding the money supply faster than output grows produces persistent inflation. The Weimar and Zimbabwe hyperinflations are extreme cases.

Modern macro views these as overlapping rather than rival explanations. Short bursts can be cost-push; sustained inflation needs accommodating monetary policy.

concepts.title: Types of Unemployment
concepts.contentHtml:
Not all unemployment is the same.

Frictional: people between jobs — short-term, healthy in a dynamic economy where workers shop around for matches.

Structural: a mismatch between worker skills and available jobs. Coal miners in a green-energy transition, factory workers displaced by automation. Persistent and painful.

Cyclical: tied to recessions — demand collapses, firms lay off. Rises and falls with the business cycle.

Classical: caused by wages held above market-clearing — minimum wages, union bargaining, efficiency wages.

The unemployment rate (BLS U-3) counts only people actively job-hunting. Broader measures (U-6) include discouraged workers and involuntary part-time. Headline rates can hide a lot.

concepts.title: The Phillips Curve
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1958 A.W. Phillips plotted UK money wage inflation against unemployment over a century and found a strong negative relationship. The Phillips curve — lower unemployment, higher inflation — became the foundational tradeoff of postwar macro policy.

Then came the 1970s. The US (and most of the West) saw simultaneous high unemployment and high inflation: stagflation. The simple Phillips curve was dead.

Friedman and Phelps had already explained why. The tradeoff existed only when expectations lagged. Once workers and firms expected inflation, they built it into wage contracts and prices, and the central bank had to deliver ever-higher inflation to keep unemployment below its natural level. The curve shifts up.

The modern expectations-augmented version: π = π^e − β(u − u*), where u* is the natural rate. In the long run, π = π^e and u = u* — no exploitable tradeoff.

concepts.title: NAIRU & the Natural Rate
concepts.contentHtml:
The natural rate of unemployment (or NAIRU, non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment) is the level the economy gravitates toward when expectations have caught up — a mix of frictional and structural unemployment.

Below NAIRU, labor markets overheat and inflation accelerates. Above it, slack pulls inflation down. Central banks effectively target NAIRU when setting policy.

Trouble is, NAIRU isn't observable. Estimates drift over time as labor markets change — globalization, demographics, unionization, gig work all move it. The 2010s saw US unemployment fall well below pre-crisis NAIRU estimates without inflation rising, leading economists to revise the number downward. The post-2021 inflation surge then pulled it back up. Policy has to act on a moving, fuzzy target.

title: Aggregate Supply & Demand
description: Short-run vs long-run, IS-LM, the AD-AS framework

concepts.title: Aggregate Demand
concepts.contentHtml:
The aggregate demand (AD) curve shows total spending in the economy at each price level. It slopes downward — but for different reasons than a microeconomic demand curve.

Three forces: the wealth effect (higher prices erode the real value of money holdings, so people spend less), the interest rate effect (higher prices raise money demand, pushing rates up and investment down), and the exchange rate effect (higher domestic prices make exports less competitive).

AD shifts with anything affecting C, I, G, or net exports — fiscal stimulus, consumer confidence, investment animal spirits, foreign demand.
mathExpressions: AD: Y = C(Y-T) + I(r) + G + NX(e)

concepts.title: Short-Run Aggregate Supply
concepts.contentHtml:
Short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) slopes upward: higher prices induce more output. Why? In the short run, wages and many other costs are sticky — set in contracts, slow to renegotiate. When prices rise but wages haven't caught up, profit margins widen and firms produce more.

SRAS shifts with input cost shocks (oil, raw materials), productivity changes, and expected inflation. The 1970s oil shocks shifted SRAS leftward, producing higher prices and lower output simultaneously — stagflation.

concepts.title: Long-Run Aggregate Supply
concepts.contentHtml:
Over enough time, wages and prices adjust fully. The long-run aggregate supply (LRAS) curve is vertical at potential output Y* — the level the economy can sustain given its labor force, capital stock, and technology.

The implication: in the long run, demand-side policy can move prices but not output. Print more money, and you eventually just get higher prices. Real growth comes only from supply-side factors — productivity, labor force growth, capital accumulation, institutions.

This was Friedman's core point and why most macroeconomists are 'monetarist in the long run, Keynesian in the short run.'

concepts.title: The IS-LM Model
concepts.contentHtml:
Hicks's IS-LM (1937) translates Keynes into a tractable diagram of two markets clearing simultaneously.

IS curve (Investment = Saving): combinations of interest rate r and output Y where the goods market clears. Slopes downward — lower r boosts investment, raising Y.

LM curve (Liquidity = Money): combinations where the money market clears given a fixed money supply. Slopes upward — higher Y raises money demand, raising r.

Their intersection gives the short-run equilibrium (r, Y). Fiscal expansion shifts IS right (higher Y, higher r). Monetary expansion shifts LM right (higher Y, lower r). Useful pedagogy, though modern macro mostly works with newer models that derive these relations from microfoundations.

concepts.title: Putting It Together: AD-AS Dynamics
concepts.contentHtml:
The AD-AS framework explains business cycles as movements around long-run potential.

A negative demand shock (financial crisis, confidence collapse) shifts AD left. Output falls, prices fall, unemployment rises. The economy is below Y*. Over time, wages fall, SRAS shifts right, output recovers — but only if the adjustment is allowed to happen.

A negative supply shock (oil crisis) shifts SRAS left. Output falls, prices rise — stagflation. There's no easy fix: stimulating demand worsens inflation, fighting inflation worsens unemployment.

The whole apparatus exists to ask one question: should policy intervene, or wait for self-correction? Keynesians say the long run is too long (wages are too sticky, suffering is too high). Classicals say intervention has its own costs and risks (timing, unintended consequences). Real central banks live with both intuitions.

title: Fiscal Policy
description: Government spending, taxation, multipliers, and crowding out

concepts.title: What Fiscal Policy Is
concepts.contentHtml:
Fiscal policy is the use of government spending and taxation to influence the economy. The two levers: spending (G) directly enters AD; taxes (T) indirectly affect AD through disposable income.

Expansionary fiscal: raise G, cut T, or both. Boost demand, reduce unemployment. Typically deployed in recessions.

Contractionary fiscal: cut G, raise T. Cool demand, fight inflation. Politically painful — voters dislike both halves.

The fiscal stance can be discretionary (deliberate policy) or automatic (built-in stabilizers like unemployment insurance and progressive taxes that adjust without legislation).

concepts.title: The Multiplier
concepts.contentHtml:
$1 of government spending doesn't add just $1 to GDP. It pays a contractor, who pays workers, who buy groceries, who pay grocers, and so on. Each round adds something more.

The simple Keynesian spending multiplier: 1/(1−MPC), where MPC is the marginal propensity to consume. If households spend 80% of new income, the multiplier is 5. $1 of G adds $5 to GDP — in theory.

The tax multiplier is smaller in absolute value: −MPC/(1−MPC). Tax cuts work less well per dollar than spending, because some of the tax cut gets saved instead of spent.

Real-world multiplier estimates are far smaller than textbook formulas — often 0.5 to 1.5 — because of leakages (imports, savings, taxes), monetary offset, and crowding out.

concepts.title: Crowding Out
concepts.contentHtml:
Government borrowing isn't free. To fund deficit spending, the government issues bonds, competing with private borrowers for the same pool of savings.

Result: interest rates rise, private investment falls — crowding out. The fiscal stimulus reaches Y, but partly by displacing I rather than just adding net new demand.

How much crowding out? Depends on the state of the economy. In deep recession with idle resources and zero-lower-bound interest rates, crowding out is small — there's plenty of slack savings to go around. At full employment, it's substantial. This is why Keynesians defend stimulus in slumps but rarely in booms.

An open-economy variant: deficit borrowing attracts foreign capital, strengthens the currency, and crowds out exports — Mundell-Fleming.

concepts.title: Debt & Sustainability
concepts.contentHtml:
Run deficits long enough and you accumulate debt. The question isn't whether debt is bad — it's whether it's sustainable.

The arithmetic: debt-to-GDP ratio stabilizes when the primary surplus equals (r − g) times the existing ratio, where r is interest rate and g is growth rate.

If g > r, you can run primary deficits forever without exploding debt — the situation in much of the developed world from 2010 to 2021. If r > g, even balanced primary budgets see the debt ratio creep up.

Sovereign debt crises happen when bond markets lose faith — Greece 2010, Argentina repeatedly. Countries with their own currency (US, UK, Japan) face less acute risk because they can in extremis monetize debt — at the cost of inflation. Currency-union members and emerging markets borrowing in foreign currency don't have that escape.

concepts.title: Ricardian Equivalence & Limits
concepts.contentHtml:
Robert Barro's provocative claim: tax cuts financed by borrowing don't stimulate spending, because rational households know they'll have to pay higher taxes later to service the debt. They save the windfall instead of spending it. Government debt is just deferred taxation.

If Ricardian equivalence holds perfectly, deficit-financed stimulus is impotent. Reality is somewhere in between: liquidity-constrained households, finite horizons, and uncertainty mean tax cuts do raise spending — but not dollar for dollar.

The bigger lesson: fiscal policy is constrained by expectations, debt levels, monetary regime, and the cyclical state of the economy. The crude Keynesian model treating G as a free lever is too simple. Modern macro takes the lever seriously while acknowledging it's stiffer and noisier than textbooks suggest.

title: Monetary Policy
description: Interest rates, money supply, the Taylor rule, zero lower bound

concepts.title: How Central Banks Set Rates
concepts.contentHtml:
The central bank's main lever is the policy rate — the interest rate at which commercial banks lend to each other overnight. In the US it's the federal funds rate; in the eurozone, the deposit facility rate; in the UK, Bank Rate.

The Fed historically set this rate by buying or selling Treasuries to adjust the supply of bank reserves — open market operations. Post-2008, with banks holding huge excess reserves, the dominant tool became interest on reserves (IOR): the Fed simply sets the rate it pays on reserves, and that becomes the floor for the funds rate.

The policy rate then ripples through other rates — short-term Treasury bills, mortgage rates, business loans, credit cards — though imperfectly and with lags.

concepts.title: Transmission Mechanism
concepts.contentHtml:
How does a change in the policy rate affect the real economy? Several channels operate at once.

Interest rate channel: lower rates make borrowing cheaper → more investment, more durable goods purchases, more housing.

Asset price channel: lower rates raise the present value of future cash flows → higher stock and house prices → wealth effect on consumption.

Exchange rate channel: lower domestic rates make the currency less attractive → it depreciates → exports become more competitive.

Credit/bank lending channel: lower rates and easier reserves make banks more willing to lend, especially to bank-dependent borrowers (small firms).

Expectations channel: if the central bank credibly signals easier policy ahead, long rates fall and confidence rises.

The lags are long and variable — Friedman's classic warning. Effects on output peak roughly a year out, on inflation closer to two.

concepts.title: The Taylor Rule
concepts.contentHtml:
John Taylor's 1993 observation: a simple formula tracked the Fed's actual rate decisions remarkably well.

The Taylor rule: r = r* + π + 0.5(π − π*) + 0.5(y − y*). Roughly — set the rate to the equilibrium real rate plus current inflation, then adjust for the inflation gap and the output gap.

Two implications worth noting. First, the response to inflation is greater than 1: a 1pp inflation overshoot triggers a 1.5pp rate hike. This Taylor principle is essential for stability — if the central bank doesn't raise real rates when inflation rises, inflation expectations spiral.

Second, no central bank follows the rule mechanically. It's a benchmark, useful for evaluating policy retrospectively and for guiding judgments about whether current policy is loose or tight.

concepts.title: The Zero Lower Bound
concepts.contentHtml:
What happens when the policy rate hits zero — and inflation is still too low and unemployment too high?

You can't easily go below zero (people would withdraw cash to avoid negative interest). The zero lower bound (ZLB) binds, and conventional policy is exhausted. Japan hit this in the 1990s; the US, UK, and eurozone all hit it post-2008.

Three unconventional tools emerged. Quantitative easing (QE): the central bank buys long-dated bonds to push down long rates directly, bypassing the policy rate. Forward guidance: commit to keeping rates low for an extended period, lowering expected future rates. Negative rates: a few central banks (ECB, SNB, BoJ) actually crossed the zero line, charging banks to hold reserves.

Effectiveness has been debated. Most economists agree these tools work, but with diminishing returns and side effects (asset bubbles, inequality from asset price inflation).

concepts.title: Independence & Inflation Targeting
concepts.contentHtml:
Most modern central banks operate as independent institutions — making rate decisions free from short-term political pressure.

The case for independence: politicians have a chronic incentive to push for low rates before elections, generating short-term booms and long-term inflation. Removing the lever from politicians' hands reduces this time-inconsistency problem. Empirically, more-independent central banks have produced lower inflation without higher unemployment.

The dominant framework since the 1990s is inflation targeting: a public commitment to a numerical inflation rate (usually 2%), with policy adjusted to hit it over the medium term. Anchoring expectations is the goal — when households and firms believe the central bank will keep inflation near target, they don't build inflation into wage demands or prices, and small shocks die out.

Independence has come under political pressure recently — populist movements challenge it, and large balance sheets blur the line between monetary and fiscal policy. The institutional consensus of 1990–2020 may not hold for the next 30 years.

title: Long-Run Growth
description: Solow model, total factor productivity, convergence, and what makes nations rich

concepts.title: Why Growth Compounds
concepts.contentHtml:
The single most important fact in economics: small differences in growth rates compound into enormous differences in living standards.

A country growing at 2% per year doubles GDP per capita in about 35 years. A country growing at 5% doubles in 14 years and is about 18× richer than the 2% country after 100 years.

This is why long-run growth dwarfs business-cycle macro in welfare terms. Recessions are painful but temporary. Differences in growth rates over decades determine whether you live in South Korea or North Korea, in 1700-style poverty or 2020s comfort.

concepts.title: The Solow Model
concepts.contentHtml:
Robert Solow's 1956 model: output Y comes from labor L, capital K, and technology A. Y = A·F(K, L).

Capital accumulates from saving (a fixed share of output) and depreciates each period. As K grows, output grows — but capital exhibits diminishing returns. Each new factory adds less than the last.

Eventually, new investment just covers depreciation, and K stops growing. The economy settles into a steady state with constant capital per worker.

Three predictions. Higher saving raises the steady-state level of output but not its long-run growth rate. Population growth lowers steady-state output per worker (more people share the capital). Technological progress is the only thing that produces sustained per-capita growth in the long run.

concepts.title: Total Factor Productivity
concepts.contentHtml:
If capital and labor explain only part of output, the rest is total factor productivity (TFP) — the residual that captures technology, organization, institutions, and how efficiently inputs are used.

Solow famously showed in 1957 that most of the growth in US output per hour worked over the previous four decades came from TFP, not from accumulating more capital or workers. We weren't just using more stuff — we were using stuff better.

TFP is the messy bucket. It includes innovation, but also management practices, financial system depth, rule of law, infrastructure, the level of education embodied in workers. Cross-country, TFP differences explain most of the gap between rich and poor nations — far more than capital differences.

concepts.title: Convergence — Or Not
concepts.contentHtml:
Solow's model predicts convergence: poor countries should grow faster than rich ones, because capital's marginal product is higher where capital is scarce. Eventually they catch up.

The data is mixed. Among rich OECD countries since 1960, convergence is real and visible — Italy and Spain closed much of the gap with the US and Germany. East Asia (Japan, Korea, Taiwan, China) converged dramatically.

But many poor countries — much of sub-Saharan Africa, parts of Latin America — have diverged, falling further behind. Convergence isn't automatic; it's conditional on countries having similar fundamentals: institutions, education, savings, openness.

'Why nations fail' (Acemoglu-Robinson) and the rise of growth empirics in the 1990s focused attention on this conditional convergence and the institutional preconditions for catching up.

concepts.title: Endogenous Growth & Ideas
concepts.contentHtml:
Solow's model treats technology A as exogenous — falling from the sky. The endogenous growth theories of Romer, Lucas, Aghion-Howitt, and others made it part of the model.

Key insight: ideas are non-rivalrous. Once invented, a recipe, formula, or design can be used by everyone simultaneously without diminishing returns. Unlike capital, ideas don't run into bottlenecks.

This produces increasing returns at the level of the world economy. Investment in R&D, education, and human capital generates ideas that benefit everyone forever. Patents and IP regimes try to give inventors enough return to incentivize discovery while still letting ideas spread.

Romer's 2018 Nobel-winning version: growth comes from research effort. Charles Jones's later work showed research productivity is itself falling — we're throwing more researchers at the problem and getting fewer breakthroughs per researcher. Whether this means we'll eventually run out of growth, or just need to keep scaling research, is one of the big open questions in macroeconomics.
